assessment.nobel_worthiness: The optical lattice clock combines Katori's magic-wavelength idea (trapping many neutral atoms so the light shift cancels in the clock transition) with Ye's realization of Sr clocks at the 1e-18 level. It is a fundamental advance in precision measurement: it tests time dilation across millimetres, constrains drifts of constants and opens the way to a redefinition of the second. It is the kind of conceptual idea that turns into measurable physics with enormous accuracy, and it connects directly to atomic structure theory I know well.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice and made the first demonstrations; Ye's group led the performance race and the quantum-many-body clock. Two laureates give a clean configuration. Hall and Hansch (comb) and Wineland (ion clocks) were already recognized, so this is a natural continuation. Contributions of others (Lemonde, Derevianko, Ludlow) are real but secondary.
assessment.maturity: Independently reproduced by several laboratories worldwide (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, SYRTE, PTB, NIST, others) with mutually consistent comparisons and a roadmap to redefinition of the second. Mature and timely.
uncertainties: Whether the committee prefers to credit the lattice idea and the clock realization separately; Lemonde, Derevianko and others could be argued to deserve mention.
I rely on my own knowledge of the field's history and have not verified exact priority dates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realize Hubbard models with tunable parameters, with the observation of the superfluid-Mott insulator transition and later Fermi-Hubbard physics, single-site imaging and thermalization studies. This gave a genuinely new way of studying quantum many-body physics where the Hamiltonian is known, and it answers questions in condensed matter from an atomic-physics setting. It builds on the 2001 BEC prize and 1997 cooling prize and is a clearly fundamental, not technologically driven, contribution.
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with Jaksch) proposed the Bose-Hubbard realization, Greiner and Bloch observed the Mott transition, and Esslinger led the fermionic work. A three-person prize is possible but any choice leaves out important people (Zoller, Ketterle-style contributors, Gross, Bakr). I choose experimental realizers here; alternatively the theory proposal could be credited and the committee might prefer Zoller over Esslinger.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced by many groups and a very active, stable field; recognition is arguably timely or slightly overdue. Quantum simulation claims of beyond-classical advantage remain a separate matter.
uncertainties: Allocation among Bloch, Greiner, Esslinger and Zoller is a real dilemma and overlaps with the separate quantum-computing candidates with Zoller and Cirac.
Whether the quantum simulation of Hubbard models is regarded as a discovery or as a platform.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Matter-wave interferometry with atoms and molecules shows directly that whole atoms behave as waves, which speaks to where the quantum-classical boundary lies, and it has become a precision tool for gravity, rotation and tests of the equivalence principle. The 1991 demonstrations (Mlynek, Pritchard, Chu/Kasevich) are conceptually clean and later sensitivity improvements are substantial.
assessment.attribution: Early demonstrations came near-simultaneously from Mlynek's double slit with atoms, Pritchard's grating interferometer, and Kasevich and Chu's light-pulse interferometer. Chu already received the 1997 prize for cooling, which complicates his omission or inclusion. Kasevich, Pritchard and Mlynek is a plausible trio but priority across the groups is shared.
assessment.maturity: Many groups have reproduced and extended the technique, and applications in gravimetry are established. Fundamental tests (equivalence principle, G, fine structure constant) are still being improved, so some of the most striking payoff is still ahead.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 1997 prize and Chu's role.
Whether the physics is considered a discovery or a development of techniques.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Squeezed light lets one beat the standard quantum limit in interferometry. Caves' 1981 analysis showed how vacuum fluctuations limit interferometers, and squeezing has been used in GEO600 and LIGO to improve sensitivity. This is a conceptually clear and practically important example of quantum noise engineering with direct relevance to the gravitational-wave detections already recognized.
assessment.attribution: Caves is the key theorist; Kimble's group made the first squeezed-state generation in cavities and extended it, and Schnabel led implementation in GEO600 and later detectors. Mavalvala's contributions to LIGO squeezing are significant and arguably fit the story, and Slusher's 1985 observation is not on the credited list, so the allocation is contested.
assessment.maturity: Squeezing is routine in current gravitational-wave detectors and confirmed by independent groups; recognition is reasonably timely, though the observational impact is incremental on top of the LIGO prize.
uncertainties: Unclear whether the committee views this as a discovery or as an enabling improvement.
Priority of the first squeezing experiments (Slusher and colleagues) is not on the credited list.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The discovery of a Higgs boson at 125 GeV in 2012 provided the missing piece of the Standard Model and was achieved by two independent, enormously demanding experiments. It is a landmark confirmation of the mechanism recognized in 2013. I defer to the particle physicists on its ranking, but the scientific importance is not in doubt.
assessment.attribution: The prize configuration is the central problem: the discovery was by collaborations of thousands, and credit could go to the initiators and leaders of ATLAS and CMS (Jenni, Della Negra, Virdee, Gianotti as spokesperson at announcement). Any set of three omits someone from the four credited, and whether a prize can fairly single out individuals here is an unresolved question for the committee.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed by both experiments and by ongoing couplings measurements at the LHC; stable interpretation and timely, although the 2013 prize partly addressed it.
uncertainties: Whether to recognize individual leaders rather than the collaborations, and which of the four credited names.
I have limited expertise in experimental particle physics and defer to colleagues.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The quantum spin Hall effect and topological insulators are a new phase of matter defined by topology rather than symmetry breaking, with the theoretical prediction followed by the clean HgTe experiment showing edge conduction. It has influenced a wide area of condensed-matter physics and links to the earlier topological prize in 2016.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the theoretical prediction; Molenkamp's group did the HgTe experiment (with the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal, and the late Shoucheng Zhang, not credited here). The configuration with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp is plausible but leaves out Bernevig and Hughes, and Zhang is deceased. Another candidate on the list bundles quantum anomalous Hall with the same people, so the boundary between topics is unclear.
assessment.maturity: Many independent confirmations (HgTe, InAs/GaSb, 3D materials by ARPES) and an established field; recognition is mature.
uncertainties: Attribution between the Kane-Mele and BHZ proposals is contested.
Overlap with the separate quantum anomalous Hall candidate.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene revealed unexpected correlated insulators and superconductivity in a tunable system whose flat bands were predicted by Bistritzer and MacDonald. This is a case where theory predicted something and experiment found much more. It opened the field of moire quantum matter, which is conceptually new.
assessment.attribution: The prediction of flat bands (Bistritzer-MacDonald) and the 2018 experiments from Jarillo-Herrero's group are decisive; Cao and others are not credited. Three names are available but Bistritzer's contribution is a single paper and others could be argued.
assessment.maturity: The field is only about eight years old; correlated phenomena are reproduced by several groups, but mechanisms of superconductivity remain unsettled, so the recognition may be premature.
uncertainties: The mechanism of superconductivity is unresolved.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Rydberg blockade supplies strong controllable interactions between neutral atoms, and optical-tweezer arrays use it for programmable quantum simulation and gates. For an atomic-structure theorist this is an elegant use of highly excited states, and it is shaping quantum simulators and computers.
assessment.attribution: The blockade proposal (Jaksch, Lukin and colleagues) and the first demonstrations (Browaeys, Saffman and others, plus Gaetan et al. and Urban et al.) are spread across many people, and the credited names do not obviously cover the original proposal. Lukin's role spans proposal and experiments, but allocation is uncertain.
assessment.maturity: Several groups have realized and scaled the approach and it is progressing quickly; still evolving, and parts of the story (error-corrected computing) are not yet settled, so recognition may be early.
uncertainties: Rapid ongoing developments make the long-term significance unsettled.
Credit for the blockade proposal versus experiment is spread among more people than the credited list.
